title: Design Top K youtube videos
summary: Exact top-K over billions of daily views is a counting and windowing problem, not a sorting problem. This guide builds a bucketed-counter design that survives hot keys and sliding windows.

blocks.title: What the interviewer is really testing
blocks.text: Nobody cares if you can sort. They care if you can **count at 1M+ events/sec without melting, then serve top-K in milliseconds across sliding windows**. This is a test of three judgments: **exact vs approximate**, **write-sharding vs read-merging**, and **where you put time**. Get those right and every follow-up becomes easy. Get them wrong and you drown in hot keys.
The problem

Design a service that continuously ingests a firehose of video view events and answers one query fast: **what are the top-K most-viewed videos for the last hour, day, month, and all-time?** Each event is essentially a `videoId` plus a timestamp. Reads are `GET /top?k=10&window=1h` style. Writes dwarf reads by 1000:1 or more. The query must return in well under a second, stay available when a single video goes viral, and handle late, duplicate, and out-of-order events without corrupting ranks.

items: `recordView(videoId, timestamp, userId?)` — fire-and-forget ingest, idempotent against retries.
`getTopK(k, window)` — returns ordered list of `{videoId, count}` for `window` in `{1h, 24h, 30d, all-time}`, where `k <= 100` typically.
Windows are **sliding**, not calendar-aligned. A query at 14:37 for `1h` means `[13:37, 14:37)`. That one word changes the entire storage design.

blocks.text: Clarify before you design
Top-K is deliberately under-specified. Small answers fork the architecture completely, so force the decisions in the first five minutes. Do not start drawing boxes until you have these.

items.title: Exact or approximate?
items.text: Do ranks have to be perfectly correct at every second? For leaderboards and monetisation, usually yes for small K and no for the tail. Exact costs 10x more. Propose exact for top-100 with bounded staleness (e.g. 1 minute) and say so explicitly.

items.title: What counts as a view?
items.text: One play event? 30 seconds watched? Unique per user per day? Deduplication rule decides whether you need per-user state or can blindly increment. Agree: count qualified views only, dedupe by eventId at ingest.

items.title: Scale and K range?
items.text: How many views per day, how many distinct videos, what K? Assume ~70B views/day (~800k avg rps, 2-3M peak), ~10B distinct videos over years, K <= 100. If the interviewer gives different numbers, redo the math out loud.

items.title: Freshness and latency SLO?
items.text: Can top-K lag by 60 seconds? Can getTopK take 200ms p99? Almost always yes. That concession lets you move from online sorting to micro-batch precomputation — the core trade-off of the whole problem.

items.title: Which windows really slide?
items.text: Is 1h sliding by the second, or tumbling every minute? True per-second sliding is brutally expensive. Most production systems quantise to 1-minute buckets and accept ~1 minute error. Get permission for that.

blocks.text: Requirements

blocks.caption: Scope agreed before drawing architecture.
rows: Ingest view events at millions rps with at-least-once delivery
Serve getTopK(k, window) ordered by count, k up to 100
Small K enables heap-merge instead of global sort
Forces bucketed counters, not single totals
No hot-key collapse when one video gets 5% of traffic
Tolerate duplicates, late and out-of-order events

blocks.text: Approach 1 — the naive approach and why it dies

The obvious answer is a relational table `views(videoId PRIMARY KEY, count)` plus `UPDATE views SET count = count+1 WHERE videoId=?` on every view, then `SELECT ... ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT K`. It is correct on a whiteboard and catastrophic in production for three independent reasons. First, the hot key: a viral video concentrates millions of writes per minute onto one row, serialising on a single partition and timing out everything behind it. Second, the sort: ordering billions of rows on every query is a full-table sort you cannot index your way out of, because the sort key mutates constantly. Third, windows: a single cumulative counter cannot answer last-hour vs last-day without storing history, so you either rescan raw events (too slow) or you have no answer at all. Trade-off named: **naive optimises for code simplicity and sacrifices write scalability, read latency, and time-travel — all three SLOs that actually matter**.

blocks.title: Never propose this without killing it
blocks.text: If you draw a single SQL counter and a global ORDER BY, interviewers mark you down unless the next sentence is why it fails. Say it fast: **single-row increments cannot absorb viral skew, and global sorts cannot serve at read time**. Then move to sharded counting plus pre-aggregated buckets.
The real design: bucket, shard, pre-merge

Stop thinking sort-then-limit. Think **count in small time buckets, then sum buckets and keep only the top-K**. Split time into fixed 1-minute buckets per video: `count(videoId, minute)`. A 1-hour window is the sum of 60 buckets; a 24-hour window is 1440 buckets. This turns a sliding-window problem into 60-1440 point lookups plus a merge, which is cheap if you only track candidates. Writes go through a durable log into a stream processor that increments bucket counters with sharded writers to defeat skew. Reads never touch the event stream — they hit a Top-K serving layer that maintains precomputed leaderboards refreshed every 30-60 seconds. Trade-off named: **you trade ~1 minute of freshness for 100x cheaper reads and immunity to hot keys**. That is almost always the right trade for a leaderboard.

blocks.title: End-to-end write and read paths
blocks.caption: Writes are buffered and aggregated; reads are served from precomputed leaderboards.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  C[Clients / Playback Events] --> G[API Gateway / Ingest]
  G --> K[(Kafka - view-events)]
  K --> S[Flink / Streaming Aggregator]
  S --> B[(Cassandra - bucket counts)]
  S --> R[(Redis - leaderboard cache)]
  B --> T[Top-K Builder - periodic job]
  T --> R
  U[Dashboard / API] --> R
  U --> B

blocks.text: Ingest is a classic log-first pipeline. Playback servers emit `{eventId, videoId, ts}` to Kafka partitioned by `hash(videoId)` with extra salting for celebrities — append a random shard suffix to the key of the top 0.01% of videos so one partition does not saturate. Flink consumes with 10-30 second micro-batches, dedupes by `eventId` in a RocksDB state store, drops late events beyond a 5-minute watermark into a side output, and emits increments to Cassandra as `INCR bucket(videoId, minute)`. Cassandra is chosen because it absorbs massive counter writes and wide-row time ranges well; the trade-off is that its counters are hard to make exactly-once, which is why dedupe happens upstream in Flink, not in the database. A separate Top-K Builder runs every 30 seconds per window, scans only plausible contenders, computes sums with a bounded heap, and writes the frozen top-500 per window into Redis. Reads are a single Redis lookup plus an optional live-delta patch from the last partial minute.
Data model and storage choices

Use two stores because no single store is good at both high-rate increments and ordered top-K serving. Cassandra holds history: row key `(videoId, window_granularity)`, clustering column `minuteTs`, value `count`. TTL the 1-minute buckets after 35 days so storage stays bounded; all-time totals live in a separate compacted table updated by batch rollup, not on the hot path. Redis holds serving state: `ZSET top:1h`, `ZSET top:24h` with score equal to window count, refreshed wholesale by the builder to avoid read-modify-write races. Back-of-envelope: 70B views/day is ~48M per minute across ~5M active videos. Storing one 16-byte counter per active video per minute is ~80MB/min of new counter data before replication — large but trivial for a Cassandra cluster, and reads only fetch the few thousand candidates tracked by the builder, not all 5M. Trade-off: **you pay 2-3x write amplification and duplicate storage to make reads O(K log N_candidates) instead of O(total videos)**.

blocks.title: Core services and stores
blocks.caption: Separation of counting, history, and serving keeps each path independently scalable.

blocks.text: Working code — the only algorithm that matters

Interviewers do not want Kafka configs. They want the merge logic that turns bucket sums into top-K without scanning every video. The pattern is: maintain a candidate set from the previous leaderboard plus recent heavy hitters, re-score only those, keep a min-heap of size K. Full rescoring of billions of keys never happens. Below is the builder core in Java and a sketch of the streaming bucket updater in Python. Both fit on a whiteboard and prove you understand why reads stay cheap.

blocks.code:
from collections import defaultdict
# Micro-batch aggregator: collapse 10s of raw events into one bucket write.
# Trade-off: 10-30s extra lag for 100x fewer DB writes. Always take it.
buckets: dict[tuple[str, int], int] = defaultdict(int)
seen_ids: set[str] = set()  # in prod: RocksDB + TTL, not memory

def on_event(event_id: str, video_id: str, minute_ts: int):
    if event_id in seen_ids:
        return  # dedupe retry / double-play
    seen_ids.add(event_id)
    buckets[(video_id, minute_ts)] += 1

def flush(store):
    for (video_id, minute_ts), delta in buckets.items():
        store.incr(video_id, minute_ts, delta)  # sharded write
    buckets.clear()

blocks.text: Complexity

blocks.caption: Costs are in buckets and candidates, never in total events.
rows: Batched in memory, one sharded counter write per bucket per flush
C = candidates (~10k), B = buckets in window (60 / 1440)
Single Redis ZREVRANGE; no DB scan on hot path
TTL minute buckets; all-time kept separately
Dedupe state bounded by 5-min watermark + TTL

blocks.text: Concurrency and the hardest follow-up: hot keys and exactness

Two failures kill most candidates. First, viral skew: one video doing 100k rps will saturate a single Kafka partition and a single Cassandra row if you key naively by `videoId`. Fix it with key salting — writers append `shard = random(N)` to the key (`videoId#shard`), Flink sums N shards at flush time, and no single writer or partition exceeds `total/N`. You pay N times more counter rows and a slightly more expensive read-merge; that is the price of surviving virality. Second, exactness under retries: at-least-once delivery plus blind increments double-counts. Fix it with idempotency upstream: every playback event carries a UUID, Flink dedupes within the watermark horizon, and Cassandra only sees collapsed bucket deltas. Late events past the watermark do not patch the frozen leaderboard — they land in the bucket store and appear at the next rebuild. State this bluntly: **true real-time exact top-K over a sliding window at YouTube scale does not exist; every production system is bounded-staleness plus bounded-candidate exactness**. Interviewers promote candidates who name that limit instead of hand-waving it.

blocks.title: The trap: true sliding windows
blocks.text: If you sum 1-minute buckets, a query at 14:37:20 covers a partial first and last bucket. Either **pro-rate the edge buckets or accept ~1 minute of error** — say which. Candidates who claim per-second precision with minute buckets lose credibility instantly.
Follow-ups to have ready

items.title: Per-country / per-category top-K?
items.text: Do not multiply the whole pipeline. Add dimensions to the bucket key: (videoId, country, minute). Storage grows by cardinality of the dimension — say that cost out loud and suggest limiting to top countries only.

items.title: Unique viewers instead of raw views?
items.text: Counting distinct users needs HyperLogLog per bucket, not counters. Merging HLLs gives ~1% error. Trade-off: exact uniques would require per-user sets — infeasible at this scale.

items.title: Fraud / view farming?
items.text: Cap views per user per video per day in Flink, flag velocity anomalies, quarantine suspicious shards. Never let filtering block the hot path — do it as a side-output that subtracts.

items.title: All-time top-K for years?
items.text: Do not sum minute buckets back to 2005. Maintain a separate cumulative table updated by daily batch rollup, rebuilt with a heap over monthly rollups. Different SLO, different pipeline.

items.title: Sudden spike alerts (trending)?
items.text: Compare short-window rate vs long-window baseline per candidate. Reuse the same bucket store with a velocity ratio — no new ingest needed, just a second builder query.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state unprompted

items: Duplicate delivery: same `eventId` arrives twice — dedupe in stream state, never in Redis.
Late event past watermark: write to bucket store, skip frozen leaderboard, converge on next rebuild.
Partial edge buckets at query time: document pro-rating vs truncation.
Ties at rank K: deterministic tie-break by `videoId` so pagination is stable.
Video deleted or made private: tombstone in serving layer; filter at read, purge lazily from history.
Cold start: empty candidate set on deploy — seed from batch rollup, not from live traffic.
Clock skew across playback servers: bucket by event time, not processing time, with watermark grace.

blocks.text: What you are graded on

blocks.caption: Weak answers describe boxes. Strong answers quantify trade-offs.
rows: Sharded bucket counters + micro-batch collapse, names hot-key limit
Fixed minute buckets summed per window, edge-bucket policy stated
Periodic heap-merge over bounded candidates into Redis ZSET
70B/day -> ~1M rps, sizes bucket storage and rebuild cost
Event IDs, watermark, idempotent flush, staleness bound stated

blocks.title: Your 45-minute plan
blocks.text: 0-5: pin exactness, view definition, K, freshness. 5-10: back-of-envelope (rps, storage, read QPS). 10-25: write path — Kafka, salted keys, Flink dedupe, Cassandra buckets. 25-35: read path — candidate heap-merge, Redis ZSET, live-delta patch. 35-45: hard follow-ups — hot keys, HLL uniques, per-country fan-out, fraud. Close with the honest line: **bounded staleness plus bounded candidates is how every real top-K ships**.
